paras: The expulsion of Will Morrison from Coulterville, Illinois, took place on August 16, 1920, when unidentified persons burned the home of Morrison, a Black mine employee, and forced him out of the Randolph County mining town. The burning followed a walkout by white miners who would not work with him, and several Black families were reported to have left afterward. Some papers reported a "race riot" with shooting, which town officials denied.

According to a St. Louis dispatch in the Rock Island Argus, miners of the Perry County Coal Corporation refused to work with Morrison in a shaft where all but two of the miners were white. The company's president, John Henderson, said he could not get a clear version of the trouble. The Phoenix Tribune's correspondent named the employer as the "West Virginia Coal company."

In the Phoenix Tribune's account, the operators drove Morrison to the "East" pit on a Friday and again on Saturday, and both times the white miners refused to go down with him. On the third try the cage operator refused to carry Morrison into the mine and was discharged, and the miners left their work, a walkout the Argus put at 300 men and the Chicago Defender at 200. Within a few hours Morrison's home was burned and he was ordered out of town.

According to the East St. Louis Daily Journal, the "unidentified citizens" who set the fire did not beat Morrison, and he complied with the order to leave. The Chicago Defender instead said the miners, angered that one of their number had been "fired," set Morrison's home afire and that other houses burned. The Phoenix Tribune reported that all Black residents were ordered to leave town.

Mayor George T. Robinson and Marshal J. W. Gillespie said they did not know the cause or who was involved and expected no further disorder. Someone appealed to the United States marshal at Springfield, and an investigation was reported ordered, though the town officials said they did not know of the appeal. As of August 17 no arrests had been made, and no later report of charges or of the investigation's result appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press story, sourced to Coulterville officials, ran on August 17 under headlines such as "DRIVE OUT NEGRO" (Bisbee Daily Review), "MOB BURNS HOME OF NEGRO; DRIVEN FROM CITY" (Amarillo Daily News) and "NEGRO MINER DEPORTED." (Memphis News Scimitar). Illinois papers wrote of a "NEAR RACE RIOT" and explained the miners' refusal to work with Morrison. A rival version from railroad men and an Illinois Central train crew, printed by the Omaha Daily Bee and the Wauwatosa News, described a riot in which a Black man and woman were shot and blamed "the importation of negroes to work in the mines."

Black weeklies took up the story from August 21. The Chicago Whip said the home was burned "by a mob" and that the mayor and marshal "pretended to know nothing" of the cause. The Chicago Defender's front page, "MINERS BURN NOMES [HOMES]; WOMEN FLEE CITY," named the miners as the attackers. The Dallas Express reprinted the wire story under "NEGRO MINER'S HOME IS BURNED BY MOB," and the Phoenix Tribune ran its own report headed "ACCEPTS WORK ONLY TO HAVE HIS HOME DESTROYED BY FIRE." Where the wire copy left the attackers unnamed, these Black papers tied the burning to the white miners' refusal to work beside Morrison.

The shooting reports were secondhand, and the mayor and marshal, the only local sources quoted, said Morrison's case was the sole basis for talk of a racial outbreak. Most accounts mention only Morrison's home, while the Defender said three homes burned. The Dallas Express printed the August 16 wire text under an August 26 dateline, and the Phoenix Tribune dated the fire "Tuesday"; both appear to be later datings of the same event.

reader.title: Expulsion of Will Morrison from Coulterville, Illinois
bases: Unidentified persons burned Will Morrison's home and ordered him out of town after white miners refused to work with him, and Black families were reported to have fled (A4, A7, A22); the burning was the means of an expulsion with a labor cause.

The AP account from town officials (A5), a separate St. Louis follow-up (A7) and the Phoenix Tribune's own Coulterville correspondent (A22) agree that Morrison's home was burned and he was driven out; only the train-crew claims of shooting (A6, A15) are contested.

accounts.label: Railroad men and Illinois Central train crew
accounts.gist: A race riot between whites and Blacks broke out; a Black man and woman were reportedly shot and their house burned, the trouble caused by importing Black workers to the mines.

accounts.label: St. Louis follow-up dispatch
accounts.gist: Perry County Coal miners refused to work with Morrison in a nearly all-white shaft; the cage operator who refused to carry him was fired, and 300 miners walked out; several Black families then left.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: The miners, angered at the firing, went to Morrison's home and set it afire; three homes burned and women and children fled.

accounts.label: Phoenix Tribune correspondent
accounts.gist: Operators tried on three days to put Morrison in the East pit; white miners refused, the cage operator was fired, the miners walked out, and within hours his home burned; all Black residents were ordered to leave.

Illinois papers used 'NEAR RACE RIOT' and 'HAS NEAR RIOT' and explained the miners' refusal to work with Morrison.
Chicago Whip said the home was burned 'by a mob' and that officials 'pretended to know nothing'.
Chicago Defender front page 'MINERS BURN NOMES [HOMES]; WOMEN FLEE CITY' named the miners as the attackers.
Dallas Express printed the AP text under 'NEGRO MINER'S HOME IS BURNED BY MOB'.
Phoenix Tribune special headed 'ACCEPTS WORK ONLY TO HAVE HIS HOME DESTROYED BY FIRE', tying the burning to his being put to work.
